implementation_notes: An object declaration is the well-known object and a map is the store: object ServiceRegistry holding a private mutableMapOf (or ConcurrentHashMap when registration can happen concurrently), with register and lookup functions - kotlinlang.org's own object-declarations page uses a provider register/list example of exactly this shape. What replaces the classic Registry class is the object declaration: instance management (lazy, thread-safe, one per class loader) is language-provided. The classic class is justified when per-instance registries are needed or when the registry should be injected rather than global.
pitfalls: An object is one instance per class loader: two copies of the library or a child class loader produce two registries, so registrations are not shared.
mutableMapOf is not thread-safe; registration after start-up needs ConcurrentHashMap or a Mutex, even though the underlying map is otherwise just a hash table.
Casts at lookup (as? T) are unchecked and yield null or ClassCastException for a mismatched key/type pair; prefer a typed token or registry per service type.

java.util.ServiceLoader cannot instantiate Kotlin objects (they have no public no-arg constructor visible to reflection), so packaging an object as a service requires a class proxy that delegates to it.
